newsitem.title: ITALY: Pope ready for appendix surgery.
newsitem.headline: Pope ready for appendix surgery.

text.p: A frail Pope John Paul prepared for surgery on Tuesday amid fierce speculation that there may be more to his illness than an inflamed appendix.

The 76-year-old Polish Pontiff, who this month celebrates 18 years as leader of the world's Roman Catholics, was due to have an operation to remove his appendix early on Tuesday, the Vatican and doctors said.
A medical bulletin on the outcome of the operation, which the Vatican has said is taking place because of a recurring inflamed appendix, was expected around 0900 GMT.

Doctors said the Pope was patient and calm as he underwent a battery of preparatory examinations on Monday, including blood and urine tests, an electrocardiogram, an echo-doppler to monitor the quality of blood flow and a chest X-ray.
"He's a good patient. I don't think he's very happy to be having these tests," said one senior medical source at Rome's Gemelli hospital, where the Pontiff was admitted late on Sunday.
"No one likes to be in a hospital, would you?"

Doctors said Professor Francesco Crucitti, who will lead the medical team, would decide late on Monday exactly how many doctors would take part in the operation. It will be the fourth time the Pontiff has undergone abdominal surgery in 15 years.
The "Pilgrim Pope" has repeatedly said he wants to lead the Catholic Church into the third millennium and has kept up a punishing schedule despite frequently appearing to be in pain.
Polish Cardinal Jozef Glemp told Vatican Radio on Monday evening he hoped the Pope "can quickly return to his mission and next year take his awaited trip to Poland".

Three fevers since Christmas have interrupted his duties and the severe trembling in his left hand, which the Vatican has until recently related to the aftermath of an assassination attempt in 1981, seemed almost out of control on Sunday.
Italian newspapers now openly speculate that the Pope is suffering from Parkinson's disease, a neurological disorder. The Vatican has not denied such reports.

Other doctors, watching the Pontiff's condition from a distance, say appendix problems are not common in elderly people and believe he may have another intestinal tumour. He had a growth the size of an orange removed in 1992, which the Vatican said was starting to turn malignant but had been caught in time.
His most senior aide, Secretary of State Cardinal Angelo Sodano, dismissed such suggestions on Sunday as "medical fiction".

Doctors say the Pope's previous abdominal operations -- two after Crucitti and other surgeons saved his life when a gunman shot him in St Peter's Square and one to remove the tumour -- meant he had internal scarring that made the operation trickier.
But the chief cardiologist on the Pope's medical team, Professor Attilio Maseri, pronounced his heart completely fit.
"Everything is fine," he said. "He's okay, he's not okay with limitations." He said cardiac complications from the surgery were "totally unpredictable".

Television crews and reporters from all over the world have poured into the university hospital in Rome's northeast suburbs, where the Pope is being treated in a heavily-guarded suite on the 10th floor, with key aides and nuns in attendance.
The Vatican said he had celebrated mass on Monday morning with Monsignor Stanislaw Dziwisz, his private secretary.
Dziwisz later joked with a reporter who asked about the Pope's condition: "If I tell you he's fine, you wouldn't believe me anyway. Don't worry."
Barring complications, the Pope is expected to stay in hospital for some five days prior to convalescence.

Corrado Manni, who is expected to be the chief anaesthetist at the operation, said the Pope's medical history could cause complications. The surgery is expected to be carried out by traditional incision rather than modern, keyhole surgery.

"Every operation carries a certain amount of risk, especially in a patient who obviously, and unfortunately...has suffered the sort of vicissitudes that have brought the present Pontiff to the Gemelli," Manni told Italian radio on Monday.
